title: The Educated Barbarian series: Book of Five Rings analysis (part. 3)
summary: Third part of his reading of Musashi's Book of Five Rings (finishing the Ground Book), applying each maxim to lifting and life: use every 'weapon' before concluding a muscle can't grow, reject victim mentality, infer many ideas from one, don't have a favourite lift or copy idols, recognize your biases, mind the long-term 'background timing' of natural progress, believe that the way is in training, learn from other strength sports, teach clearly, and attend to small details.

claims.claim: Musashi's line about not dying with your weapon undrawn applies to lifting: if one method fails for your arms, change volume, intensity, tonnage, exercises, angles or weighted stretches before concluding they can't grow; you can't run out of options.
Giving up has become cool; victim mentality is addictive and comfortable because nothing is ever your fault, whether genetics, environment or circumstances.
'From one thing, ten thousand things': don't just absorb information but infer further ideas from it, and don't become a fanboy who treats one idea as gospel, including his own videos.
Once you walk a Way, you see it in everything; he draws inspiration for bodybuilding from everywhere, and people who excel at a hobby tend to be obsessed with it.
Don't have a favourite lift or method: favouritism is emotional, blinds you to whether it's good for you, and makes people treat critics of their lift as enemies.
Strive for proficiency (doing the lift comfortably, easily, without injury) in every lift, not just one, by researching movement patterns, specificity and synergy.
YouTube fitness teaches people to copy idols and switch to a new one every six months, which damages self-improvement; take inspiration but find your own way, and don't copy him either.

He partly disagrees with Musashi on having no likes and dislikes: humans are subjective, so accept your biases, recognize them as your way rather than the right way, and watch for agendas you're unaware of.
Understanding and matching the rhythm of your life is a path to happiness, though nobody can explain exactly how.
For an already-developed natural, gains happen in the 'background timing' over months; focusing only on today's session and losing sight of the program and its goal leads to mistakes.

As a football cornerback he had tunnel vision and was often beaten on reverses, but basketball came easier because he already could keep his head up; field of vision is partly talent and broadens with practice.

Saying you can't achieve anything without drugs or with bad genetics is dishonest; the Way is in training, and believing training does nothing makes it so. Train hard and consistently and let the way find you.
His progress was slow and took 10 years, but he keeps going because the Way is in training.
He follows powerlifting and strongman and learns from them despite lacking the talent or passion for them, because they are also moving bodies through space.
If you can't explain a concept clearly, you're a bad teacher or don't fully understand it, not a tortured genius.
Pay attention to small issues in your training because they accumulate over time into lost gains.

He partly disagrees with 'do nothing which is of no use': he does fun projects like finger push-ups that won't make him bigger, but such distractions should be kept to a minimum if you want to master something.
